title: Learned Routing of Latent State Between LLM Agents
kicker: Doctoral Research Direction · Multi-Agent Language Models
tools: PyTorch · Hugging Face Transformers · vLLM · Qwen3 / Qwen3.5 · Slurm on the OSU (Oregon State University) cluster · W&B (Weights & Biases)
blurb: Can LLM agents share internal state instead of text? Passing KV caches does carry information (91% vs 92% for text), but does not beat a single agent.
long: Teams of LLM agents typically communicate via text, where the worker outputs their findings token-by-token, and all recipients must process the tokens again. Agents based on the same model can instead communicate by passing internal states, like KV-cache. My NSF GRFP (National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship Program) application is for a project where a manager controls this communication, workers output compact latent space summaries, and the manager learns from team reward what summaries to give to each agent within a bandwidth limit, for teams of 8-16 agents.

First, an audit of what actually crosses. I replicated LatentMAS (published latent multi-agent method) on Qwen3-4B using GSM8K (grade school math) and ARC-Challenge (science questions), 300 questions × 3 seeds each. I verified that my implementation produced bit-identical caches and solver logits compared to the official implementation. I added controls with cache content: cache for a different question, no cache, noise cache, and sweeping number of latent steps.

The outcome is mixed, so it is reported as mixed. The latent team ties a single agent (+0.1 and −0.2 points, with 95% intervals that include zero), but the text team improves by 3.4 and 2.4 points. However, replacing it with another problem’s cache reduces performance by 4.0 and 6.2 points, and for GSM8K, 16% of the swapped arm’s errors are the answer to the other question. So information does flow through the channel, but it does not improve performance if the receiving agent can solve the problem without it.

Second, a split-information probe where communication is necessary: the sender holds a GSM8K problem's facts and the solver only its question (100 questions, one seed). The right cache scores 91%, a wrong cache or no cache 0%, and a text message 92% (difference −1.0 points, 95% interval −7 to +5). The latent sender needs 2.4× fewer estimated FLOPs (floating-point operations) per question in total and, at batch size 1, 19× less sender time than a text sender that thinks before writing. But its message is 25 MiB of KV cache against 111 text tokens, about 61,000× more bytes, so this measures context sharing, not compression. That gap is what the learned compact summaries in the proposal are meant to close.

Surrounding this is the infrastructure required by the plan: a harness for running agents in multi-turn GEM (General Experience Maker) environments, with all interactions logged to a live viewer, and an RL (reinforcement learning) pipeline using GRPO (group-relative policy optimization) with LoRA (low-rank adaptation) on SWE-smith (software engineering) bug-fixing tasks in network-isolated containers. On 59 held-out tasks × 2, Qwen3.5-4B solves 54% (64/118) and Qwen3.5-2B 16.9% (20/118). I am writing up a paper on the audit.
highlights: LatentMAS (latent multi-agent system) reproduction on Qwen3-4B, bit-identical to the official code
Latent team ties a single agent: +0.1 / −0.2 points
Wrong cache costs 4.0 / 6.2 points: content does cross
Split probe: right cache 91%, text 92%, wrong or no cache 0%
Latent sender 19× faster, 2.4× fewer total FLOPs (floating-point operations), 61,000× larger message
note: Code private · paper draft in progress
